pieces.text: All organisms have pieces of hereditary material called genes, which are passed from parents to offspring. Genes contain instructions for building the parts of an organism. An organism's genes affect its observable traits, including its appearance, its behavior, and which diseases it may have.
Genes may have different alleles, or forms, that can cause different versions of a trait.

For example, flower color is a trait in pea plants. The gene for this trait has two possible alleles. Each allele is represented by an uppercase or lowercase letter. The allele F is for purple flowers, and the allele f is for white flowers.
Each pea plant has two alleles for the flower color gene—one allele inherited from each parent.

contents.text: An organism's genotype for a gene is its combination of alleles for that gene. So, a pea plant may have a genotype of FF, Ff, or ff for the flower color gene.

An organism's phenotype for a trait is its observable version of that trait, which depends on the organism's combination of alleles. A pea plant may have a phenotype of purple flowers or white flowers for the flower color trait.

pieces.text: An organism's phenotype for a trait is its observable version of that trait.
Ranger's observable version of the fur color trait is black fur.
So, Ranger's phenotype for the fur color trait is black fur.

pieces.text: is a condition that affects mucus.

is a jelly-like substance that certain cells produce to protect the body from infection. Humans with cystic fibrosis produce mucus that is thicker and stickier than usual. This sticky mucus builds up in the lungs and interferes with breathing.
​In a group of humans, some individuals have cystic fibrosis and others do not. In this group, the gene for the cystic fibrosis trait has two alleles.
The allele for not having cystic fibrosis (F) is dominant over the allele for having cystic fibrosis (f).

subpoints.text: All organisms have pieces of hereditary material called genes, which are passed from parents to offspring. Genes contain instructions for building the parts of an organism. An organism's genotype for a gene is its combination of alleles for that gene. So, a pea plant may have a genotype of FF, Ff, or ff for the flower color gene.

subpoints.text: All organisms have pieces of hereditary material called genes, which are passed from parents to offspring. Genes contain instructions for building the parts of an organism. An organism's genes affect its observable traits, including its appearance, its behavior, and which diseases it may have. Each gene may have different alleles, or forms, that can cause different versions of a trait.

header.text: For example, flower color is a trait in pea plants. The gene for this trait has two possible alleles. Each allele is represented by an uppercase or lowercase letter. The allele F is for purple flowers, and the allele f is for white flowers. Each pea plant has two alleles for the flower color gene—one allele inherited from each parent.

contents.text: An organism's genotype for a gene is its combination of alleles for that gene. So, a pea plant may have a genotype of FF, Ff, or ff for the flower color gene.

An organism's phenotype for a trait is its observable version of that trait, which depends on the organism's combination of alleles. A pea plant may have a phenotype of purple flowers or white flowers for the flower color trait.

header.text: Some of the alleles have types called dominant and recessive. These two types can cause different versions of the trait to appear as the organism's phenotype.

contents.text: A dominant allele causes its version of the trait to appear even when the organism also has a recessive allele for the gene. In the Punnett square below, there are two parent pea plants with the genotype Ff for the flower color gene.
These parents can produce offspring with the genotype FF, Ff, or ff.

subpoints.text: Some traits, such as flower color in pea plants, are controlled by a single gene. Most plants and animals have a genotype made up of two alleles for these traits. These two alleles may have types called dominant and recessive, and they determine whether an organism is homozygous or heterozygous for the gene.

header.text: An organism with two identical alleles for a gene is homozygous for that gene.

contents.text: If both alleles are dominant, the organism is homozygous dominant. In pea plants, the F allele, which causes purple flowers, is dominant. A pea plant with the genotype FF is homozygous dominant for the flower color gene.

If both alleles are recessive, the organism is homozygous recessive. In pea plants, the f allele, which causes white flowers, is recessive. A pea plant with the genotype ff is homozygous recessive for the flower color gene.
An organism with two different alleles for a gene is heterozygous for that gene. A pea plant with the genotype Ff is heterozygous for the flower color gene.

pieces.text: In a group of cats, some individuals have straight fur and others have curly fur. In this group, the gene for the fur type trait has two alleles.
The allele for curly fur (f) is recessive to the allele for straight fur (F).

contents.text: This Punnett square shows a cross between two cats.
How many boxes represent offspring that are heterozygous for the fur type gene?

pieces.text: To determine how many boxes in the Punnett square represent offspring that are heterozygous for the fur type gene, look at the alleles.
The question tells you that the f allele, which is for curly fur, is recessive to the F allele, which is for straight fur.
So, the dominant allele for the fur type gene is F, and the recessive allele is f.

contents.text: A heterozygous genotype must have two different alleles. So, offspring that are heterozygous for the fur type gene must have the genotype Ff.
All 4 boxes in the Punnett square have the genotype Ff.

The allele F is for purple flowers, and the allele f is for white flowers. Each pea plant has two alleles for the flower color gene—one allele inherited from each parent.

subpoints.text: All organisms have pieces of hereditary material called genes, which are passed from parents to offspring. Genes contain instructions for building the parts of an organism. An organism's genes affect its observable traits, including its appearance, its behavior, and which diseases it may have. Each gene may have different alleles, or forms, that can cause different versions of a trait.

header.text: For example, flower color is a trait in pea plants. The gene for this trait has two possible alleles. Each allele is represented by an uppercase or lowercase letter. The allele F is for purple flowers, and the allele f is for white flowers. Each pea plant has two alleles for the flower color gene—one allele inherited from each parent.

contents.text: An organism's genotype for a gene is its combination of alleles for that gene. So, a pea plant may have a genotype of FF, Ff, or ff for the flower color gene.

An organism's phenotype for a trait is its observable version of that trait, which depends on the organism's combination of alleles. A pea plant may have a phenotype of purple flowers or white flowers for the flower color trait.

subpoints.text: An organism's genotype depends on the genotypes of its parents. You can use the genotypes of two parents to predict the possible genotypes of their offspring with the help of a Punnett square.

pieces.text: A Punnett square is a chart that represents a cross, or breeding event, between two organisms. This chart shows the genotypes of two parents, and all the possible genotypes of their offspring, for a specific gene.
The genotypes of the parents are shown on the top and left side of the Punnett square. The possible genotypes of the offspring are shown in the boxes inside the Punnett square.

header.text: Some of the alleles have types called dominant and recessive. These two types can cause different versions of the trait to appear as the organism's phenotype.

contents.text: A dominant allele causes its version of the trait to appear even when the organism also has a recessive allele for the gene. In pea plants, the F allele, which causes purple flowers, is dominant over the f allele. A pea plant with at least one F allele will have the F allele's version of the flower color trait. So, a plant with the genotype FF or Ff will have purple flowers.

A recessive allele causes its version of the trait to appear only when the organism does not have any dominant alleles for the gene. In pea plants, the f allele, which causes white flowers, is recessive to the F allele. A pea plant with only f alleles will have the f allele's version of the flower color trait. So, a plant with the genotype ff will have white flowers.

subpoints.text: An organism's genotype depends on the genotypes of its parents. You can use the genotypes of two parents to predict the possible genotypes of their offspring with the help of a Punnett square.

pieces.text: A Punnett square is a chart that represents a cross, or breeding event, between two organisms. This chart shows the genotypes of two parents, and all the possible genotypes of their offspring, for a specific gene.
The genotypes of the parents are shown on the top and left side of the Punnett square. The possible genotypes of the offspring are shown in the boxes inside the Punnett square.
In the Punnett square below, there are two parent pea plants with the genotype Ff for the flower color gene.
These parents can produce offspring with the genotype FF, Ff, or ff.

subpoints.text: Some traits, such as flower color in pea plants, are controlled by a single gene. Most plants and animals have a genotype made up of two alleles for these traits. These two alleles may have types called dominant and recessive, and they determine whether an organism is homozygous or heterozygous for the gene.

header.text: An organism with two identical alleles for a gene is homozygous for that gene.

contents.text: If both alleles are dominant, the organism is homozygous dominant. In pea plants, the F allele, which causes purple flowers, is dominant. A pea plant with the genotype FF is homozygous dominant for the flower color gene.

If both alleles are recessive, the organism is homozygous recessive. In pea plants, the f allele, which causes white flowers, is recessive. A pea plant with the genotype ff is homozygous recessive for the flower color gene.
An organism with two different alleles for a gene is heterozygous for that gene. A pea plant with the genotype Ff is heterozygous for the flower color gene.

subpoints.text: All organisms have pieces of hereditary material called genes, which are passed from parents to offspring. Genes contain instructions for building the parts of an organism. An organism's genes affect its observable traits, including its appearance, its behavior, and which diseases it may have. Each gene may have different alleles, or forms, that can cause different versions of a trait.

header.text: Some of the alleles have types called dominant and recessive. These two types can cause different versions of the trait to appear as the organism's phenotype.

contents.text: A dominant allele causes its version of the trait to appear even when the organism also has a recessive allele for the gene. In pea plants, the F allele, which causes purple flowers, is dominant over the f allele. A pea plant with at least one F allele will have the F allele's version of the flower color trait. So, a plant with the genotype FF or Ff will have purple flowers.

A recessive allele causes its version of the trait to appear only when the organism does not have any dominant alleles for the gene. In pea plants, the f allele, which causes white flowers, is recessive to the F allele. A pea plant with only f alleles will have the f allele's version of the flower color trait. So, a plant with the genotype ff will have white flowers.

The allele for green fruit (f) is recessive to the allele for yellow fruit (F).

contents.text: This Punnett square shows a cross between two ornamental gourd plants.
How many boxes represent offspring with green fruit?

pieces.text: To determine how many boxes in the Punnett square represent offspring with green fruit, consider whether green fruit is the dominant or recessive allele's version of the fruit color trait.
The question tells you that the f allele, which is for green fruit, is recessive to the F allele, which is for yellow fruit.
So, green fruit is the recessive allele's version of the fruit color trait.
An ornamental gourd plant with the recessive version of the fruit color trait must have only recessive alleles for the fruit color gene.
The recessive allele for the fruit color gene is f.
So, offspring with green fruit must have the genotype ff.

lessons.name: Describe the effects of gene mutations on organisms

contents.text: The following passage describes the effects of a gene mutation, which is a permanent change in a gene. Read the passage and then follow the instructions below.

elements.text: In plants such as the European cantaloupe, fruit ripening is affected by a substance called ethylene (ETH-uh-leen). Ethylene is made inside a plant's cells with the help of a protein called CmACO1. The CmACO1 protein is encoded by the CmACO1 gene.

A certain European cantaloupe plant had a mutation in its CmACO1 gene. Compared to the CmACO1 gene without a mutation, the mutated CmACO1 gene encoded a form of the CmACO1 protein with a different structure.

This different form of the CmACO1 protein could make only a small amount of ethylene. The fruits of this plant took longer to ripen than fruits from plants containing more ethylene. Farmers found this mutation useful because the fruit stayed good for a longer period of time after harvest.

elements.text: As in humans, hunger in mice depends on how much food a mouse has eaten. When a mouse eats, its hunger is controlled by the leptin receptor protein.

The leptin receptor protein receives signals from the mouse's body when the mouse eats. The leptin receptor protein then sends signals to the brain, telling it that the mouse is full. The leptin receptor protein is encoded by the OB-R gene.
A certain mouse had a mutation in the OB-R gene. Compared to the OB-R gene without a mutation, the mutated OB-R gene encoded a form of the leptin receptor protein with a different structure.

This different form of the leptin receptor protein was unable to send signals to the mouse's brain. This mouse continued to eat as if it did not feel full. As a result, the mouse ate a large amount of food and became obese.

elements.text: Cholesterol (koh-LES-ter-ol) is a fat-like substance that has many functions in the body. Cholesterol moves through the body in the blood. The amount of cholesterol in the blood is controlled by proteins, including the PCSK9 protein. The PCSK9 protein is encoded by the PCSK9 gene.
The PCSK9 protein adds cholesterol to the blood. The action of the PCSK9 protein can lead to blood cholesterol levels that may, over time, cause heart disease.
A certain person had a mutation in the PCSK9 gene. Compared to the PCSK9 gene without a mutation, the mutated PCSK9 gene encoded a form of the PCSK9 protein with a different structure.

This different form of the PCSK9 protein could add only a small amount of cholesterol to the blood. So, this person had a lower risk of developing heart disease than a person with more cholesterol in their blood.

elements.text: The hairs in a jaguar's coat are colored by molecules called pigments. The pigments are made in cells at the base of each hair. When these cells make light pigments, the hair is light-colored. When these cells make dark pigments, the hair is black.

A protein called MCR1 controls how the jaguar's cells color each hair with light and dark pigments. The function of the MCR1 protein results in jaguars with spotted coats, made up of both light-colored and black hairs. The MCR1 protein is encoded by the MCR1 gene.

A certain jaguar had a solid black coat because of a mutation in its MCR1 gene. Compared to the MCR1 gene without a mutation, the mutated MCR1 gene encoded a form of the MCR1 protein with a different structure.
This different form of the MCR1 protein allowed only dark pigments to color the hairs.

elements.text: Common carp are a type of fish that have scales on their bodies. The pattern of scales on a common carp is established while the fish is developing inside its egg. During this time, a protein called Fgfr1a1 sends signals to the fish's body that direct the shape and spacing of the fish's scales. The signals from the Fgfr1a1 protein result in common carp with small, evenly spaced scales.
The Fgfr1a1 protein is encoded by the fgfr1a1 gene.

A certain carp had large, patchy scales because of a mutation in the fgfr1a1 gene. Compared to the fgfr1a1 gene without a mutation, the mutated fgfr1a1 gene encoded a form of the Fgfr1a1 protein with a different structure.
This different form of the Fgfr1a1 protein could not send signals to the fish's body.

elements.text: Antibiotics are substances that get inside bacterial cells and cause them to die. Doctors often use antibiotics to kill bacteria that cause infections, such as Salmonella typhimurium (S. typhimurium).

Compared to the AcrB gene without a mutation, the mutated AcrB gene encoded a form of the AcrB protein with a different structure.
This different form of the AcrB protein was able to pump certain antibiotics out of the cell.

elements.text: The eyes of fruit flies look red because they contain molecules called pigments, which color the eyes red. Cells in the eyes of fruit flies have parts that make these pigments from other molecules.

elements.text: Keratins are strong proteins that provide structure and protection for many tissues in the human body. For example, the tissue on the inside of the mouth, called epithelium (ep-i-THEEL-i-um), is protected by a tough layer made of many types of keratin proteins connected together. pieces.text: . Genes are a hereditary material, which means they are passed from parents to offspring. Genes are located inside cells on structures called chromosomes.

header.text: Genes and the environment affect an organism's growth and development in different ways:

contents.text: Genes contain information that cells use as instructions. These instructions tell cells how to build an organism's parts and how to carry out other biological processes. Different types of organisms have different sets of genes.

The environment provides the raw materials that an organism uses to grow and carry out biological processes. These raw materials include food, water, and other nutrients. The environment also includes conditions such as wind or high temperatures that can influence an organism's size and shape.

content.text: The specific effect of an environment on an organism does not depend on the organism's genes.

explanationText.text: A certain environmental condition may not have the same effect on all organisms. The way an organism responds to an environmental condition often depends on the organism's genes.

content.text: An organism's environment always affects how the organism grows.

explanationText.text: As an organism grows, it steadily takes in raw materials and is constantly exposed to the conditions in its surroundings. So, an organism's growth is always affected by its environment.

content.text: Differences in how two organisms grow can be due mainly to genetic factors or environmental factors, or can be due to both.

explanationText.text: The growth of all organisms depends on both genetic factors and environmental factors. Two organisms can grow differently because they have different genes, because they are in different environments, or both. This means that differences in how two organisms grow can be due mainly to genetic factors or environmental factors, or can be due to both.

content.text: The growth and development of all organisms are influenced by their genes.

explanationText.text: All organisms have genes that provide the instructions for building the organisms' parts and controlling biological processes.
